Merrily
MER-i-lee
adv. (in high spirits; Haman's wife's counsel, to build the gallows and then go in merrily to the banquet)
From Old English myrge, pleasant. At Esther 5:14 it renders Hebrew sameach, glad or joyful — here the gladness of a man whose enemy is about to hang.

Biblical Definition

The word appears once, and the sentence it appears in is one of the most chilling in Scripture: Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made. The counsel is precise about the order of events. Build the gallows first; get the warrant in the morning; then enjoy the dinner. Haman's wife understood that her husband's trouble was not the empire but one Jew who would not bow, and that the party would be spoiled until he was dealt with.

What follows is Scripture's most exact piece of reversal. That same night the king could not sleep and called for the chronicles; Haman came in the morning to ask for the hanging and was made to lead Mordecai through the street in the king's apparel; and by evening: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Fifty cubits, built to his own specification. The book of Esther never once names God, and every turn of it is His hand — the sleepless night, the chronicle opened at the right page, the queen's courage, the gallows standing ready. Solomon's law holds in the one story that does not mention the Lawgiver: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): with mirth; with gaiety and laughter; jovially.

expand to see more

MERRILY, adv. With mirth; with gaiety; with laughter; jovially; cheerfully.

MERRY, a. Gay and noisy; jovial; exhilarated to laughter; cheerful.

GALLOWS, n. An instrument of punishment, on which criminals are put to death by hanging.

BANQUET, n. A feast; a rich entertainment of meat and drink.

CUBIT, n. In anatomy, the fore arm; in Scripture, a measure of length, about eighteen inches.

Key Scripture

Esther 5:14 — "Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made."

Esther 7:10 — "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified."

Proverbs 16:18 — "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."

Proverbs 15:13 — "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken."

Modern Corruption

Esther is read as a tale of coincidence or of human courage alone, when the absence of God's name in the book is the whole point of how the book teaches providence.

expand to see more

Esther never names God, and two bad readings follow from it. One treats the book as essentially secular — a court story of nerve and luck that made it into the canon by accident of national sentiment. The other over-corrects and inserts God into every verse as though the narrator had merely forgotten. The book itself does something more skilful than either: it removes the name and lets the reader watch a chain of events no one could have arranged — a sleepless night, a chronicle opened at one page, a gallows built to the wrong height for the wrong man — until the conclusion is unavoidable. Providence is demonstrated rather than asserted, which is exactly how most believers experience it.

Zeresh's counsel is worth naming for its own sake. She proposed that her husband settle a grudge before dinner so the dinner could be enjoyed, and Scripture records that the thing pleased Haman. This is what malice does to pleasure: it cannot rest while one man in the gate refuses to bow, and it will spend a fortune in timber to be able to eat in peace. The gallows fifty cubits high is the measure of how much a proud man's happiness depended on one Jew's knee, and how little was left of it when the knee stayed straight.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sameach (H8056), glad; ets (H6086), a tree or gallows; mishteh (H4960), a banquet or drinking-feast.

expand to see more

Hebrew sameach (H8056) — glad, joyful; the adverb the AV renders merrily.

Hebrew ets (H6086) — a tree, timber; the word for the gallows Haman built.

Hebrew mishteh (H4960) — a feast, from the verb to drink; the banquets that frame the whole book.

Hebrew gaon (H1347) — pride; what Haman had, and what the proverb says goes before a fall.

Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, to overturn; the book's own word for the reversal of the ninth of Adar.

Usage

"“then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet” — settle the grudge, then enjoy dinner."

"“And the thing pleased Haman” — four words that seal him."

"“they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared” — built to his own specification."
